domain_name: Scope and reach of the Act

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Stated purpose
questions.question: A compliance trainer at a newly listed retailer quotes the long title of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002. Which purpose does that title MOST directly state?

options.A: To create the SEC to oversee securities markets and exchanges
options.B: To protect investors through more accurate and reliable corporate disclosures
options.C: To have Congress set the accounting standards issuers must follow
options.D: To protect investors by requiring audited statements from every U.S. company

questions.key_concept: The Act's long title states its purpose: to protect investors by improving the accuracy and reliability of corporate disclosures.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the Act set out to fix, and which companies the securities laws actually reach.
questions.correct_explanation: The long title of Public Law 107-204 says the Act exists to protect investors by improving the accuracy and reliability of corporate disclosures made under the securities laws. Option D shares the investor-protection aim but misstates the reach: the Act's duties fall on issuers in the SEC reporting system, not on every U.S. company. Private companies outside that system file no SEC reports.

wrong_explanations.A: The SEC was established by Section 4 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, decades before SOX. The Act gives the SEC new rulemaking and enforcement work instead.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the Act deals with accounting. But Section 108 lets the SEC recognize a private standard setter's principles; the SEC recognized the FASB in 2003.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it shares the investor-protection aim, but the Act reaches issuers in the SEC reporting system, not every U.S. company, so private companies have no SOX filings.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the SEC dates from the 1934 Exchange Act, and C, because accounting standards come from a standard setter the SEC recognizes.
Final two: B beats D because the Act's duties fall on issuers, not on every U.S. company; its stated aim is reliable disclosure by companies in the reporting system.
Exam cue: when an item asks why SOX exists, look for the long title's words: protecting investors through accurate and reliable corporate disclosures.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Enforcement
questions.question: The SEC finds that an issuer's officers broke an SEC rule adopted under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. Under Section 3(b), how is that violation treated?

options.A: A matter for the PCAOB to investigate and discipline
options.B: A breach of state corporate law, pursued by the company's home state
options.C: A Securities Act of 1933 violation, with that Act's penalties
options.D: An Exchange Act of 1934 violation, with that Act's penalties

questions.key_concept: Section 3(b) treats a violation of the Act, its SEC rules or PCAOB rules as a violation of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
questions.pre_read: Recall which federal securities statute the Act borrows its enforcement framework from.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 3(b)(1) says a violation of the Act, of SEC rules issued under it or of PCAOB rules is treated for all purposes as a violation of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, with the same penalties. Option C names the wrong statute: the Securities Act of 1933 governs offerings, while the Exchange Act is the enforcement framework the Act borrows.

wrong_explanations.A: The PCAOB registers, inspects and disciplines audit firms of issuers. It does not enforce SEC rules against an issuer's officers; the SEC does.
wrong_explanations.B: SOX is federal securities law. Section 3(b) routes its violations into the Exchange Act's federal enforcement scheme, not into state corporate law.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it names a federal securities statute, but Section 3(b) borrows the Exchange Act of 1934, not the Securities Act of 1933, which governs offerings.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the PCAOB oversees audit firms rather than issuers, and B, because SOX is federal law enforced by the SEC.
Final two: D beats C because Section 3(b) ties SOX violations to the Exchange Act of 1934, the statute that governs reporting companies.
Exam cue: when an item asks how a SOX breach is enforced, think SEC and Exchange Act penalties, not a new agency or a separate code.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Companies affected and which provisions apply. Pre-offering status
questions.question: Halvern Labs, a private company, has filed a Securities Act registration statement for its first offering; it is not yet effective or withdrawn. Under Section 2(a)(7), what is Halvern's status now?

options.A: It is already an issuer while the statement is pending
options.B: It becomes an issuer once its shares list on an exchange
options.C: It becomes an issuer when the statement becomes effective
options.D: It becomes an issuer once its revenue passes $100 million

questions.key_concept: Under Section 2(a)(7), a company with a filed, pending and unwithdrawn Securities Act registration statement is already an issuer.
questions.pre_read: List the routes by which a company becomes an issuer, then ask whether this company has already taken one.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 2(a)(7) defines an issuer to include a company that files or has filed a Securities Act registration statement that has not yet become effective and has not been withdrawn. Halvern is therefore an issuer now, before any sale. Option C is the near miss: effectiveness starts the Section 15(d) reporting duty, but issuer status under the Act begins with the filing itself.

wrong_explanations.B: Exchange listing is one route (Section 12), but a pending registration statement, Section 12(g) or a Section 15(d) duty also makes a company an issuer.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: effectiveness triggers Section 15(d) reporting, yet the Act's definition already covers a filed statement that is pending and not withdrawn.
wrong_explanations.D: The Act's definition of issuer has no revenue or size test. Revenue thresholds appear in the filer categories, not in whether a company is an issuer.

tips: Eliminate: B, because listing is only one of the routes into issuer status, and D, because the issuer definition has no size test.
Final two: A beats C because Section 2(a)(7) covers a registration statement that is filed but not yet effective, as long as it is not withdrawn.
Exam cue: issuer status has three routes: Section 12 registration, a Section 15(d) duty, or a pending registration statement. Check each before deciding.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Companies affected and which provisions apply. Filer category thresholds
questions.question: A controller at a manufacturer that has filed two annual reports, and was never an accelerated or large accelerated filer, applies Rule 12b-2. Which float range makes it an accelerated filer, other conditions met?

options.A: From $60 million up to under $560 million
options.B: Any public float under $250 million
options.C: From $75 million up to under $700 million
options.D: Any public float of $700 million or more

questions.key_concept: Under Rule 12b-2, an accelerated filer has a public float of $75 million or more but under $700 million, with the other conditions met.
questions.pre_read: Rule 12b-2 uses more than one pair of float numbers. Ask which pair applies to a company entering a category.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 12b-2 defines an accelerated filer by a public float of $75 million or more but less than $700 million, measured on the last business day of the second fiscal quarter, plus a reporting history and failing the revenue test. Option A mixes up the exit thresholds: $60 million and $560 million apply only to issuers already in a category, so a company that was never accelerated uses the entry range.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: $60 million to under $560 million is where a large accelerated filer drops back to accelerated status; entry uses $75 million to under $700 million.
wrong_explanations.B: A float under $250 million is the smaller reporting company test, which sets scaled disclosure, not the accelerated filer range.
wrong_explanations.D: A float of $700 million or more marks a large accelerated filer, the category above accelerated filers.

tips: Eliminate: B, the smaller reporting company float test, and D, the large accelerated filer threshold.
Final two: C beats A because $75 million and $700 million are the entry thresholds; $60 million and $560 million govern leaving a category.
Exam cue: entry and exit thresholds differ on purpose, so a company does not flip categories each year. Read whether the item asks about entering or leaving.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Companies affected and which provisions apply. Internal control report content
questions.question: Brightwell Tools is a non-accelerated filer, not an emerging growth company, filing its third Form 10-K. Under Section 404, what must that annual report contain?

options.A: Management's assessment and the auditor's attestation on it
options.B: No internal control report until it becomes an accelerated filer
options.C: The auditor's attestation in place of management's own assessment
options.D: Management's internal control assessment, with no auditor attestation

questions.key_concept: A non-accelerated filer includes management's 404(a) assessment but is exempt from the auditor's 404(b) attestation under Section 404(c).
questions.pre_read: Separate management's duty from the auditor's duty, then ask which of the two depends on filer status.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 404(a) requires management's internal control report in each annual report filed under Section 13(a) or 15(d); Item 308's instructions excuse only a newly public company's first annual report. Section 404(c), added by Dodd-Frank Section 989G(a), removes the auditor's 404(b) attestation for issuers that are neither accelerated nor large accelerated filers. Option A would be right for an accelerated filer that is not an emerging growth company.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: this is the full requirement for accelerated and large accelerated filers. Section 404(c) removes the auditor attestation for a non-accelerated filer.
wrong_explanations.B: Section 404(c) exempts non-accelerated filers only from 404(b). Management's 404(a) assessment applies to every annual report after the first.
wrong_explanations.C: The auditor attests to management's assessment; it never replaces it. And a non-accelerated filer needs no auditor attestation in the first place.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the exemption covers only the auditor's part, and C, because an attestation reports on management's assessment rather than replacing it.
Final two: D beats A because Section 404(c) removes the 404(b) attestation for issuers that are neither accelerated nor large accelerated filers.
Exam cue: 404(a) follows the annual report; 404(b) follows filer status. Settle the filer category before deciding whether the auditor attests.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Companies affected and which provisions apply. Overlapping statuses
questions.question: Corvane Bio listed three years ago, still qualifies as an emerging growth company, and is now an accelerated filer under Rule 12b-2. Must its auditor attest under Section 404(b)?

options.A: No; emerging growth companies are excluded from the attestation
options.B: Yes; its accelerated filer status brings the auditor's attestation
options.C: Yes; that exemption ends after its second annual report
options.D: No; the newly public company transition period still applies

questions.key_concept: An emerging growth company is excluded from the 404(b) auditor attestation even when its float makes it an accelerated filer.
questions.pre_read: Two statuses apply to this company at once. Check how each one affects the auditor's role.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 404(b), as amended by the JOBS Act, requires the auditor's attestation for each issuer other than an emerging growth company. Corvane keeps that status until a Rule 12b-2 end event, such as high revenue or becoming a large accelerated filer, so no attestation is required. Option B states the general rule for accelerated filers, but the statute's EGC carve-out overrides it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: accelerated filers normally need the attestation, but Section 404(b) excludes emerging growth companies, so the EGC status controls here.
wrong_explanations.C: EGC status does not lapse after two annual reports. Rule 12b-2 ends it on events such as high revenue, large debt issues or large accelerated filer status.
wrong_explanations.D: Item 308's transition covers only a company's first annual report. Corvane listed three years ago, so that relief has passed.

tips: Eliminate: C, because EGC status ends only on the Rule 12b-2 events, and D, because the newly public relief covers only the first annual report.
Final two: A beats B because the EGC carve-out in Section 404(b) applies even when the company's float makes it an accelerated filer.
Exam cue: when two statuses overlap, check each exemption separately; an EGC that is an accelerated filer still skips the auditor attestation.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Companies affected and which provisions apply. Registered funds
questions.question: The compliance officer of a mutual fund registered under Section 8 of the Investment Company Act is scoping Section 404. Which conclusion is MOST accurate for the fund?

options.A: Management reports on internal control, but the auditor does not attest
options.B: The auditor attests, but management files no internal control report
options.C: Neither management's report nor the auditor's attestation applies
options.D: Both apply once the fund's net assets exceed $75 million

questions.key_concept: Section 405 exempts registered investment companies from Sections 401, 402 and 404, including both parts of the internal control report.
questions.pre_read: Find the section that speaks to registered funds, then read how far its exemption reaches.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 405 says nothing in Sections 401, 402 or 404, or the SEC rules under them, applies to an investment company registered under Section 8 of the Investment Company Act of 1940. So neither the 404(a) management report nor the 404(b) attestation applies. Option A treats the fund like a non-accelerated filer, but the fund's exemption comes from Section 405 and covers all of Section 404.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: this is the pattern for a non-accelerated filer under Section 404(c). A registered fund falls under Section 405, which removes all of Section 404.
wrong_explanations.B: An auditor's attestation reports on management's assessment, so it cannot stand alone. And Section 405 removes both parts for a registered fund.
wrong_explanations.D: Section 405 has no asset threshold. The $75 million figure is the Rule 12b-2 float entry point for accelerated filers, which does not apply here.

tips: Eliminate: B, because an attestation needs management's assessment to report on, and D, because Section 405 has no size threshold.
Final two: C beats A because Section 405 removes all of Section 404 for registered investment companies, not just the auditor's attestation.
Exam cue: Section 405 names exactly three sections for registered funds: 401, 402 and 404. Other provisions are untouched by it.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Companies affected and which provisions apply. Filer status in practice
questions.question: Under Rule 12b-2 as amended in 2020, Pellora Foods has reported for three years, with a $300 million public float and $60 million in annual revenues. Must its auditor attest to internal control?

options.A: Yes; its $300 million float makes it an accelerated filer
options.B: No; the revenue test makes it a non-accelerated filer
options.C: Yes; any issuer with three years of reports needs it
options.D: No; issuers under $100 million revenue are exempt from Section 404

questions.key_concept: An issuer with revenues under $100 million and a float under $700 million is not an accelerated filer, so 404(b) does not apply.
questions.pre_read: Work through every condition of the accelerated filer definition, not only the float.
questions.correct_explanation: Since the SEC's 2020 amendments, Rule 12b-2 excludes from the accelerated filer category any issuer eligible for smaller reporting company status under the revenue test: annual revenues under $100 million and a float under $700 million. Pellora meets that test, so it is a non-accelerated filer and Section 404(c) removes the auditor attestation. Option A applies the float range alone and misses the revenue test.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the float is in the $75 million to $700 million range, but Rule 12b-2 also requires failing the revenue test, which Pellora passes.
wrong_explanations.C: Reporting history is one condition for accelerated filer status, not a trigger on its own. Attestation depends on filer category and EGC status.
wrong_explanations.D: The revenue test removes only the auditor's 404(b) attestation. Management's 404(a) assessment still belongs in each annual report after the first.

tips: Eliminate: C, because reporting history alone does not set filer status, and D, because management's own 404(a) report still applies.
Final two: B beats A because Rule 12b-2 keeps issuers that pass the revenue test out of the accelerated filer category, whatever their float.
Exam cue: for filer status, check float, then reporting history, then the revenue test; low revenue can override a mid-sized float.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Foreign private issuers. Status test
questions.question: Kestrel Mining, an Australian-incorporated company run from Perth, has 60% of its voting shares held by U.S. residents and mostly U.S.-citizen directors. Is Kestrel a foreign private issuer under Rule 3b-4?

options.A: No; it meets the U.S. ownership test and one contact test
options.B: Yes; incorporation outside the U.S. settles the question
options.C: No; any U.S. shareholding removes foreign private status
options.D: Yes; its business is run from Australia, which keeps the status

questions.key_concept: A foreign issuer loses FPI status when U.S. residents hold over 50% of its voting securities and any one contact test is met.
questions.pre_read: Separate the ownership condition from the business-contact conditions before deciding.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Rule 3b-4(c), a foreign issuer is not a foreign private issuer if more than 50% of its voting securities are held of record by U.S. residents and any one contact test is met. Kestrel meets the ownership condition, and a majority of its directors are U.S. citizens, which is one contact test. Option D wrongly treats the contact tests as cumulative; meeting one is enough.

wrong_explanations.B: Incorporation abroad makes Kestrel a foreign issuer, the first step. Rule 3b-4(c) then removes private-issuer status when the ownership and contact conditions are met.
wrong_explanations.C: U.S. shareholding matters only above 50% of voting securities, and then only together with a contact test. Small U.S. holdings change nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: its administration is outside the U.S., but Rule 3b-4(c) needs only one contact test, and director citizenship already meets it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because incorporation abroad is only the first step of the test, and C, because U.S. ownership counts only above 50% of voting securities.
Final two: A beats D because Rule 3b-4(c) is met by majority U.S. ownership plus any one contact test, not all three.
Exam cue: for FPI status, check U.S. ownership above 50%, then look for any one U.S. contact: officers or directors, assets, or administration.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Foreign private issuers. Annual report form
questions.question: Solvane AG, a German foreign private issuer with shares registered under Exchange Act Section 12(b), prepares its annual report. Which of these forms must it use for that report?

options.A: Form 6-K, which carries news the company publishes at home
options.B: Form 10-Q, the quarterly report that domestic issuers file
options.C: Form F-6, which registers depositary receipts on the company's shares
options.D: Form 20-F, filed within four months after the fiscal year-end

questions.key_concept: A foreign private issuer files its annual report on Form 20-F within four months of fiscal year-end; Form 6-K carries home-country news.
questions.pre_read: Think about which reports a foreign company sends the SEC during the year and which one covers the full year.
questions.correct_explanation: Form 20-F is the form foreign private issuers use for Exchange Act registration and for annual reports under Section 13(a) or 15(d), and the annual report is due within four months after fiscal year-end (Form 20-F General Instruction A.(b)). Option A is also a foreign private issuer form, but Form 6-K carries information published at home between annual reports; it is furnished, not an annual report.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Form 6-K is the foreign private issuer's form for home-country news between annual reports. It is furnished, not the annual report.
wrong_explanations.B: Form 10-Q is the domestic quarterly report. It is not a foreign private issuer's default form, and it is never an annual report.
wrong_explanations.C: Form F-6 registers depositary receipts under the Securities Act and covers only the deposit terms, with no information about the company.

tips: Eliminate: B, the domestic quarterly report, and C, the registration form for depositary receipts.
Final two: D beats A because Form 20-F is the foreign private issuer's annual report, while Form 6-K furnishes home-country news between annual reports.
Exam cue: FPI forms pair up with domestic ones: Form 20-F for the 10-K and Form 6-K for current news. Match the form to the report's purpose.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Foreign private issuers. Certification scope
questions.question: Tavira SA, a foreign private issuer, furnishes half-year results on Form 6-K and later files its annual Form 20-F. Under Rule 13a-14(a), which report must carry the officer certifications?

options.A: Both reports, since each contains the company's financial results
options.B: Neither report, since foreign private issuers are outside Section 302
options.C: The Form 20-F alone, as the annual report filed under Section 13(a)
options.D: The Form 20-F, starting when Tavira becomes an accelerated filer

questions.key_concept: Officer certifications under Rule 13a-14(a) go with Forms 10-Q, 10-K, 20-F and 40-F, not with a furnished Form 6-K.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the certification rule follows the content of a report or the form it is filed on.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 13a-14(a) requires the principal executive and financial officers' certifications in each report filed on Form 10-Q, 10-K, 20-F or 40-F. Form 6-K is not on that list: it is furnished to carry home-country information, not filed as a periodic report. Option A is tempting because the 6-K holds financial results, but the rule attaches certifications to the listed forms, not to content.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the 6-K holds financial results, but Rule 13a-14(a) lists Forms 10-Q, 10-K, 20-F and 40-F. A furnished 6-K is not among them.
wrong_explanations.B: Foreign private issuers with registered securities are issuers. Rule 13a-14(a) expressly includes Form 20-F among the reports that carry the certifications.
wrong_explanations.D: Filer status decides the auditor's 404(b) attestation, not the officer certifications. The certifications apply to every Form 20-F annual report.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Rule 13a-14(a) names Form 20-F, and D, because filer status affects the auditor attestation rather than the certifications.
Final two: C beats A because the certification rule lists the forms that need it, and Form 6-K is not one of them.
Exam cue: officer certifications attach to filed periodic reports on listed forms; a furnished Form 6-K carries none, even with financial data.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Foreign private issuers. Audit committee rules
questions.question: An exchange-listed foreign private issuer has a board of auditors, set up under home-country law, that meets every condition in Rule 10A-3(c)(3). What does the rule MOST accurately allow?

options.A: It must still form a separate audit committee of independent directors
options.B: That body may meet the listing standard instead of an audit committee
options.C: It is freed from every audit committee duty, including complaint procedures
options.D: Management may appoint and oversee the auditor directly instead

questions.key_concept: Under Rule 10A-3(c)(3), a qualifying home-country board of auditors may stand in for a foreign private issuer's audit committee for listing purposes.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a home-country body must look like for the U.S. listing standards to accept it.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 10A-3(c)(3) exempts a foreign private issuer's listing from the audit committee requirements in paragraphs (b)(1) to (b)(5) when a home-country board of auditors meets the rule's conditions, such as independence from management and responsibility for the auditor. That board then acts in place of an audit committee. Option A overlooks this accommodation, which spares issuers from duplicating a body home law already requires.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: domestic listed issuers need an independent audit committee, but Rule 10A-3(c)(3) lets a qualifying home-country board of auditors fill that role.
wrong_explanations.C: The exemption is not a release from duties. Rule 10A-3(c)(3)(vi) applies the complaint, adviser and funding requirements to the board of auditors itself.
wrong_explanations.D: A qualifying board must be independent of management and responsible for appointing and overseeing the auditor. Handing that to management breaks the conditions.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the complaint, adviser and funding duties pass to the board of auditors, and D, because auditor oversight must stay independent of management.
Final two: B beats A because Rule 10A-3(c)(3) lets a qualifying board of auditors meet the listing standard in place of an audit committee.
Exam cue: FPI accommodations change who performs a duty or when, but the duty stays. Look for the body that takes the duty over.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Registration and EDGAR. Route into reporting
questions.question: Orrin Software sold shares to the public under an effective Securities Act registration statement but never listed them. Which provision MOST directly requires Orrin to file periodic reports?

options.A: Exchange Act Section 12(b), which covers securities on national exchanges
options.B: Securities Act Section 5, which governs every sale of securities
options.C: Exchange Act Section 12(g), which covers widely held securities
options.D: Exchange Act Section 15(d), which supplements Section 13 reporting

questions.key_concept: A company whose Securities Act registration statement became effective must file periodic reports under Exchange Act Section 15(d).
questions.pre_read: Ask which fact in the stem started the company's reporting duty, and which provision ties to that fact.
questions.correct_explanation: Exchange Act Section 15(d) makes an issuer whose Securities Act registration statement has become effective file the periodic reports Section 13 requires, even without Section 12 registration. That is Orrin's route. Option C could also apply if Orrin had over $10 million in assets and enough holders of record, but the stem gives no such facts; the effective registration alone triggers 15(d).

wrong_explanations.A: Section 12(b) applies to securities registered for trading on a national securities exchange. Orrin never listed its shares, so 12(b) is not its route.
wrong_explanations.B: Securities Act Section 5 requires a registration statement before an offering. It governs the sale, not the periodic reports that follow it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Section 12(g) reaches widely held companies by asset and holder thresholds, but nothing here meets them; the effective registration triggers 15(d).

tips: Eliminate: A, because Section 12(b) covers exchange listings, and B, because Securities Act Section 5 governs the offering rather than later reports.
Final two: D beats C because Section 15(d) attaches directly to an effective registration statement, while 12(g) needs asset and holder thresholds the stem never states.
Exam cue: trace the route into reporting: listing points to 12(b), size and holders to 12(g), a completed registered offering to 15(d).

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Registration and EDGAR. EDGAR basics
questions.question: A new analyst on a listed utility's reporting team is told that the quarterly report goes on EDGAR. Which description of EDGAR is MOST accurate?

options.A: The SEC's electronic system for submitting filings and reading them
options.B: The SEC regulation that sets what an annual report must contain
options.C: The PCAOB's database of inspection reports on audit firms
options.D: The SEC system that reviews and approves each filing before release

questions.key_concept: EDGAR is the SEC's electronic filing and public access system; Regulation S-T requires periodic reports to be filed through it.
questions.pre_read: Think about what happens to a report after the reporting team finishes it.
questions.correct_explanation: EDGAR, the Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval system, is the SEC's primary system for submitting documents under the Securities Act and the Exchange Act, and the public can search it free. Regulation S-T Rule 101 requires periodic reports to be filed through it. Option D gets the system right but its job wrong: EDGAR receives and publishes filings; it does not approve them.

wrong_explanations.B: EDGAR is a system, not a rule. Regulation S-T requires electronic filing through it, and the forms and Regulation S-K set what reports contain.
wrong_explanations.C: The PCAOB publishes its own inspection reports. EDGAR belongs to the SEC and holds filings by companies and others under the securities laws.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: EDGAR is an SEC system, but it receives and publishes filings. Acceptance on EDGAR is not SEC approval; staff reviews happen separately.

tips: Eliminate: B, because EDGAR is a system rather than a content rule, and C, because EDGAR belongs to the SEC rather than the PCAOB.
Final two: A beats D because EDGAR receives filings and makes them public; it does not approve them before release.
Exam cue: separate systems from rules and from reviews. EDGAR is where filings go, Regulation S-T says they must go there, and staff review is separate.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Registration and EDGAR. Annual report deadline
questions.question: Graystone Retail is an accelerated filer, not a large accelerated filer, with a December 31 year-end. Which deadline MOST accurately applies to its Form 10-K?

options.A: 40 days after fiscal year-end
options.B: 75 days after fiscal year-end
options.C: 90 days after fiscal year-end
options.D: Four months after fiscal year-end

questions.key_concept: An accelerated filer must file its Form 10-K within 75 days after fiscal year-end.
questions.pre_read: Settle the filer category first, then recall how the annual deadline changes with size.
questions.correct_explanation: 17 CFR 249.310(b) sets Form 10-K deadlines by filer category: 60 days after fiscal year-end for large accelerated filers, 75 days for accelerated filers and 90 days for all other registrants. Graystone is an accelerated filer, so 75 days applies. Option C is the deadline for non-accelerated filers, the category below, and would leave Graystone filing late.

wrong_explanations.A: Forty days is the Form 10-Q deadline for accelerated and large accelerated filers, for each of the first three quarters, not the annual report.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: 90 days applies to registrants that are neither accelerated nor large accelerated filers. Graystone's accelerated status shortens it to 75.
wrong_explanations.D: Four months is the Form 20-F deadline for foreign private issuers' annual reports. Graystone files Form 10-K.

tips: Eliminate: A, the quarterly report deadline, and D, the foreign private issuer's Form 20-F deadline.
Final two: B beats C because accelerated filers have 75 days; 90 days is for non-accelerated filers.
Exam cue: Form 10-K deadlines step down with size: 90, 75, then 60 days. Fix the filer category before you pick the deadline.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 American Depositary Receipts. Sponsorship
questions.question: A U.S. broker-dealer asks a depositary bank to set up an ADR program for a Chilean company that relies on Rule 12g3-2(b), without the company's cooperation. Which program can the broker-dealer initiate?

options.A: An unsponsored Level 2 program listed on a U.S. exchange
options.B: A Level 3 program that raises new capital for the company
options.C: An unsponsored Level 1 program traded over the counter
options.D: No program, since every ADR program needs the company's agreement

questions.key_concept: Only a Level 1 ADR program may be unsponsored: a broker-dealer can initiate one through a depositary, without the company, for over-the-counter trading.
questions.pre_read: Ask which ADR levels need the foreign company itself to file anything with the SEC.
questions.correct_explanation: The SEC's ADR bulletin says Level 1 is the only facility that may be unsponsored, set up without the company's cooperation and often initiated by a broker-dealer. Form F-6, which the depositary files, is available when the company reports to the SEC or its shares are exempt under Rule 12g3-2(b), as here. Option A fails because a Level 2 listing needs the company itself to register and file Form 20-F.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Level 2 means an exchange listing, which requires the company itself to register and file Form 20-F reports, so it cannot be unsponsored.
wrong_explanations.B: A Level 3 program raises capital for the company through its own registration statement, such as Form F-1 or F-3, which needs the company.
wrong_explanations.D: Sponsored programs need the company's agreement, but an unsponsored Level 1 program can be initiated through a depositary without it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because raising capital needs the company's own registration statement, and D, because unsponsored programs exist without the company's agreement.
Final two: C beats A because only Level 1 may be unsponsored; an exchange listing needs the company to register and file Form 20-F.
Exam cue: if the company is not involved, think unsponsored Level 1 and over-the-counter trading; listing or raising capital needs the company.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 American Depositary Receipts. Program levels
questions.question: Velmora plc wants its ADRs listed on a U.S. national securities exchange and to raise new capital from U.S. investors in the same program. Which ADR level is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Level 2, filing Form 20-F annual reports with the SEC
options.B: Level 1, registering the ADRs on Form F-6 alone
options.C: Any level, since Form F-6 lets each program raise capital
options.D: Level 3, with a Form F-1 or F-3 offering

questions.key_concept: Only a Level 3 ADR program combines an exchange listing with raising new capital through a registered offering, such as on Form F-1 or F-3.
questions.pre_read: Match each of the company's two goals to what each ADR level permits.
questions.correct_explanation: The SEC's ADR bulletin describes Level 3 as the program that both establishes a trading presence and raises capital: the company registers the offering, for example on Form F-1 or F-3, and files annual reports on Form 20-F. Option A brings the exchange listing and Form 20-F reporting, but a Level 2 program may not be used to raise capital.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Level 2 gives the exchange listing and Form 20-F reporting Velmora wants, but a Level 2 program may not be used to raise capital.
wrong_explanations.B: Level 1 trades over the counter, files just Form F-6, and cannot raise capital, so it fails both of Velmora's goals.
wrong_explanations.C: Form F-6 covers only the terms of the deposit agreement. Raising capital needs a separate registration statement, such as Form F-1 or F-3.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Level 1 is over-the-counter with no capital raising, and C, because Form F-6 registers only the deposit terms.
Final two: D beats A because only Level 3 adds a registered offering, such as on Form F-1 or F-3, to the exchange listing.
Exam cue: ADR levels climb by market access: Level 1 over the counter, Level 2 exchange listing, Level 3 listing plus new capital.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 American Depositary Receipts. Reporting consequences
questions.question: Lunaris SA has a sponsored Level 1 ADR program traded over the counter; only Form F-6 has been filed. What is MOST accurate about Section 302 certifications for its CEO and CFO?

options.A: None are due; Lunaris files no periodic reports
options.B: They are due because its ADRs are registered on Form F-6
options.C: They are due because U.S. investors can buy its ADRs
options.D: They are due once the ADRs pass a $75 million public float

questions.key_concept: A Level 1 ADR program files only Form F-6, so the company has no periodic report carrying Section 302 certifications.
questions.pre_read: Trace which SEC filings this program produces and which duties ride on each.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 302 certifications attach to each annual or quarterly report filed under Exchange Act Section 13(a) or 15(d), and Rule 13a-14(a) lists the forms, such as Form 20-F. A Level 1 program files only Form F-6, so Lunaris has no annual report for its officers to certify. Option B fails because Form F-6 registers the deposit terms only and creates no periodic reporting.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the ADRs are registered with the SEC, but Form F-6 covers only the deposit agreement and brings no periodic reports to certify.
wrong_explanations.C: U.S. trading alone does not create SEC reporting. Certifications attach to periodic reports, and a Level 1 program files none.
wrong_explanations.D: Public float thresholds sort reporting issuers into filer categories. They do not create a certification duty for a company that files no reports.

tips: Eliminate: C, because U.S. trading alone creates no periodic reports, and D, because float thresholds sort reporting issuers rather than creating duties.
Final two: A beats B because Form F-6 registers only the deposit terms; certifications need a Form 20-F or other periodic report.
Exam cue: follow the report. No periodic report on a listed form means no Section 302 certification to sign.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. Who a provision reaches
questions.question: A warehouse manager at a privately owned logistics firm shreds shipping logs to impede a federal agency's investigation. Which provision added by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act MOST directly reaches this manager?

options.A: Section 302, the civil certification of each periodic report
options.B: 18 U.S.C. 1520, on keeping audit workpapers for five years
options.C: 18 U.S.C. 1519, a criminal statute enacted through Section 802
options.D: Section 906, the criminal certification of each periodic report

questions.key_concept: 18 U.S.C. 1519, added by Section 802, applies to any person who destroys or falsifies records to obstruct a federal matter.
questions.pre_read: Look at who each provision names as the person who can break it.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 802 of the Act added 18 U.S.C. 1519, which applies to whoever knowingly alters, destroys or falsifies records with intent to impede a federal investigation or matter, with up to 20 years in prison. It is not limited to issuers or their staff. Option D is also criminal, but Section 906 binds the CEO and CFO of an issuer filing periodic reports.

wrong_explanations.A: Section 302 requires the principal executive and financial officers of reporting companies to certify reports. A private firm's warehouse manager signs nothing under it.
wrong_explanations.B: 18 U.S.C. 1520 binds accountants who audit issuers, requiring them to keep audit or review workpapers for five years. It does not reach a private firm's warehouse manager.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: Section 906 carries criminal penalties, but it binds the CEO and CFO of an issuer filing periodic reports, not a private firm's staff.

tips: Eliminate: A and B, because Section 302 binds reporting companies' certifying officers and Section 1520 of Title 18 binds auditors of issuers, not a private firm's manager.
Final two: C beats D because 18 U.S.C. 1519 applies to whoever destroys records to obstruct a federal matter; Section 906 reaches issuers' certifying officers.

Exam cue: Section 1519 reaches whoever destroys records to obstruct a federal matter; duties tied to signing a periodic report (302, 906) or auditing an issuer (1520) reach only those signers or auditors.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. Whistleblower coverage
questions.question: A shift lead at a subsidiary whose financial information is consolidated into a listed parent's statements reports suspected shareholder fraud to their manager and is demoted. Does Section 806, as amended in 2010, protect them?

options.A: No; internal reports to a manager fall outside the statute's protection
options.B: Yes; it covers consolidated-subsidiary staff who report to a supervisor
options.C: Yes, provided they also gave the same fraud report to the SEC
options.D: No; it protects the listed parent's own staff, not any subsidiary's staff

questions.key_concept: Section 806 protects any employee of a public company or its consolidated subsidiary who reports suspected fraud, including to a supervisor.
questions.pre_read: Check who employs the shift lead and whom the report went to, then compare both with the statute's text.
questions.correct_explanation: 18 U.S.C. 1514A, added by Section 806, bars a public company, including a subsidiary whose financial information is in its consolidated statements, from demoting an employee for reporting suspected shareholder fraud to a person with supervisory authority. The shift lead is covered and the internal report is protected. Option D reflects the 2002 wording; Dodd-Frank Section 929A added consolidated subsidiaries.

wrong_explanations.A: Section 806 expressly protects reports to a person with supervisory authority over the employee, as well as reports to federal agencies and Congress.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the Dodd-Frank award program needs an SEC report. But Section 806 protects a report made just to a person with supervisory authority.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the protection starts with the listed company, but the current text expressly includes subsidiaries whose financial information is consolidated.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a report to a supervisor is a protected channel, and C, because Section 806 needs no report to the SEC as well.
Final two: B beats D because 18 U.S.C. 1514A now names subsidiaries whose financial information is included in the parent's consolidated statements.
Exam cue: for whistleblower scope, check three things: a covered company or consolidated subsidiary, an employee, and a protected report channel.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Failure and response
questions.question: A trainer tells new finance staff that executives at several collapsed companies said they never knew their reported results were wrong. Which response in the Act MOST directly targets that defense?

options.A: The auditor's report attesting to management's internal control assessment
options.B: The CEO's and CFO's own certification of each periodic report
options.C: A new board that registers and inspects public company auditors
options.D: Limits on the non-audit services an auditor may sell to clients

questions.key_concept: The Act answered executives' claims of ignorance by making the CEO and CFO personally certify each periodic report.
questions.pre_read: Ask which failure the stem describes, then which actor each option's fix binds.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 302 makes the principal executive and financial officers certify each annual and quarterly report: that they reviewed it, that based on their knowledge it has no material misstatement, and that they are responsible for its controls. A signed statement from each officer removes the 'I never knew' defense. Option A also targets reliable reporting, but it is the auditor's statement, not the executives' own.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Section 404(b) adds an outside check on internal control, but it is the auditor's statement; it does not bind the executives to the report's content.
wrong_explanations.C: Title I created the PCAOB to oversee audit firms. It answers weak audit oversight, not executives who deny knowing what their reports said.
wrong_explanations.D: Section 201 limits non-audit services to protect auditor independence. It answers conflicted auditors, not executives' claims of ignorance.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because the PCAOB and the limits on non-audit services target audit firms, not what executives know about their own reports.
Final two: B beats A because only the officer certification puts the CEO's and CFO's own signatures behind each report; the attestation is the auditor's statement.
Exam cue: match each SOX fix to the failure and the actor it binds; executives who deny knowledge point to the Section 302 and 906 certifications.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Companies named in the Act
questions.question: A compliance trainer tells new staff that the Sarbanes-Oxley Act names Enron in a provision punishing its former executives. Which correction is MOST accurate?

options.A: It names Enron in Title VIII's criminal penalties for fraud
options.B: It names Enron in Section 304's repayment of executive bonuses
options.C: It names Enron only in an SEC study of enforcement actions
options.D: It names Enron only in a GAO study of investment banks' role

questions.key_concept: The Act sets general rules; it names Enron and Global Crossing only in Section 705's study of investment banks.
questions.pre_read: Separate the Act's general duties and penalties from the studies it ordered after the scandals.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 705 directed the Comptroller General, who heads the GAO, to study whether investment banks and financial advisers helped public companies manipulate earnings, naming the collapse of Enron and the failure of Global Crossing. No penalty provision names a company. Option C is the neighboring Section 704, an SEC study of five years of enforcement actions and restatements, which names no company.

wrong_explanations.A: Title VIII's record-destruction and securities fraud crimes apply to whoever commits them. They name no company.
wrong_explanations.B: Section 304 makes the CEO and CFO of any issuer repay certain pay after a misconduct restatement. It names no company.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Section 704 did order an SEC study of enforcement actions and restatements, including off-balance-sheet entities, but it names no company.

tips: Eliminate: A and B, because the Act's penalty and repayment rules are general and apply to any person or issuer, never to a named company.
Final two: D beats C because Enron appears in Section 705's GAO study of investment banks; Section 704's SEC study names no company.
Exam cue: SOX rules are general and forward-looking; the scandals behind it are named only in the studies Title VII ordered.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Bodies the Act created
questions.question: On a SOX training quiz, a new analyst marks the SEC, the FASB and the PCAOB as bodies the Sarbanes-Oxley Act created. Which correction is MOST accurate?

options.A: The PCAOB alone; the SEC and the FASB both predate the Act
options.B: The SEC and the PCAOB; the FASB was already in place
options.C: The FASB and the PCAOB; the SEC was already in place
options.D: None of them; the Act gave new duties to existing bodies

questions.key_concept: The Act created the PCAOB; the SEC came from the 1934 Act, and the FASB predates the Act.
questions.pre_read: For each body, recall where it came from before deciding what the Act added.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 101 of the Act established the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board to oversee audits of public companies. The SEC was established by Section 4 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and the FASB was formed in 1973; in 2003 the SEC recognized its standards under Section 108. Option C credits the Act with the FASB because Section 108 deals with accounting standards.

wrong_explanations.B: The SEC dates from Section 4 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. The Act gave it new rulemaking and oversight work.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Section 108 concerns accounting standards, but it lets the SEC recognize an existing private standard setter; the FASB was formed in 1973.
wrong_explanations.D: Title I did create a new body: the PCAOB, a nonprofit corporation that oversees audits of public companies.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the SEC dates from the 1934 Exchange Act, and D, because Title I created the PCAOB.
Final two: A beats C because Section 108 recognizes an existing standard setter; the FASB was formed in 1973, long before the Act.
Exam cue: SOX created the PCAOB; it built on the SEC (1934) and recognized the FASB rather than creating either.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Companies affected and which provisions apply. Debt-only issuer
questions.question: Rowan Utilities has no public stock, but it sold bonds under an effective Securities Act registration statement and files Section 15(d) reports. Must its CEO and CFO give Section 302 certifications?

options.B: No; issuers with no public float are outside the Act
options.C: Yes; each annual and quarterly report it files needs them
options.D: Yes, but only in its annual reports, not its quarterly ones

questions.key_concept: A debt-only company reporting under Section 15(d) is an issuer, and its CEO and CFO certify each periodic report.
questions.pre_read: Find the route by which the company reports, then check which reports Section 302 names.

Rowan is an issuer under Section 2(a)(7) through its 15(d) duty, so it needs no public stock. wrong_explanations.B: Public float sorts issuers into filer categories. It does not decide whether a company is an issuer or whether Section 302 applies.
wrong_explanations.D: Section 302 applies to each annual and quarterly report. The once-a-year duty is management's internal control report under Section 404(a).

tips: Eliminate: B, because float sets the filer category, not SOX coverage, and D, because Section 302 covers quarterly reports as well.
Final two: C beats A because Section 302 names reports filed under Section 15(d) as well as Section 13(a); no stock listing is needed.
Exam cue: a Section 15(d) filer is an issuer even with debt only, and its periodic reports carry the officer certifications.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Companies affected and which provisions apply. Smaller reporting company overlap
questions.question: Fenwick Foods, reporting for four years and not an emerging growth company, has a $200 million public float and $150 million in revenues. Under current Rule 12b-2, must its auditor attest under Section 404(b)?

options.A: No; only large accelerated filers need the auditor's attestation
options.B: Yes; it is an accelerated filer even as a smaller reporting company
options.C: No; smaller reporting companies are exempt from the auditor's attestation
options.D: Yes; any issuer with revenues over $100 million needs the attestation

questions.key_concept: Smaller reporting company and accelerated filer status can overlap; an accelerated filer owes the auditor's attestation either way.
questions.pre_read: Run the float test and the revenue test separately, then decide which filer categories the company falls into.
questions.correct_explanation: Fenwick's $200 million float makes it a smaller reporting company under the float test, but its $150 million in revenues fails the revenue test, so Rule 12b-2 also makes it an accelerated filer. Section 404(c) exempts only issuers that are neither accelerated nor large accelerated filers. Option C is the common trap: smaller reporting company status alone does not remove the attestation.

wrong_explanations.A: Section 404(c) exempts only issuers that are neither accelerated nor large accelerated filers. Accelerated filers owe the attestation too.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: many smaller reporting companies are non-accelerated filers, but one that fails the revenue test with a float of $75 million or more is accelerated.
wrong_explanations.D: Revenue alone never triggers the attestation. A company with $150 million in revenues but a float under $75 million is a non-accelerated filer.

tips: Eliminate: A, because accelerated filers owe the attestation too, and D, because revenue alone never sets filer status.
Final two: B beats C because the revenue test, not the smaller reporting company label, decides accelerated status; Fenwick is both.
Exam cue: for Section 404(b), ask one question: is the issuer an accelerated or large accelerated filer that is not an emerging growth company?

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Companies affected and which provisions apply. End of emerging growth status
questions.question: An emerging growth company's CFO is tracking when its status, and so its exclusion from Section 404(b), will end. Under Rule 12b-2, which event ends that status?

options.A: Becoming an accelerated filer under Rule 12b-2
options.B: Filing its second annual report after the offering
options.C: Reaching $1.1 billion in total annual gross revenues
options.D: Being deemed a large accelerated filer under Rule 12b-2

questions.key_concept: Emerging growth company status ends, among other events, on the date the company is deemed a large accelerated filer.
questions.pre_read: Recall the events that end emerging growth company status, then test each option against them.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 12b-2 ends emerging growth company status at the earliest of four events: a fiscal year with revenues of $1.235 billion or more, the year-end after the fifth anniversary of the IPO, over $1 billion of non-convertible debt issued in three years, or the date the company is deemed a large accelerated filer. Option A is the trap: an accelerated filer can keep the status.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: accelerated filer status does not end it. Section 404(b) excludes an emerging growth company even when its float makes it an accelerated filer.
wrong_explanations.B: The status can last until the fiscal year-end after the fifth anniversary of the IPO, well past a second annual report.
wrong_explanations.C: The revenue cap is $1.235 billion (Rule 12b-2, since 2022). A company with $1.1 billion in revenues stays under it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the time limit runs to five years after the IPO, and C, because the revenue cap is $1.235 billion.
Final two: D beats A because only large accelerated filer status ends the status; an accelerated filer can stay an emerging growth company.
Exam cue: emerging growth status ends at the first of four events: $1.235 billion revenues, five years after the IPO, $1 billion of debt, or large accelerated filer.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Structure of the Act
questions.question: A compliance analyst is building a SOX training map from the Act's table of contents. Under which title does Section 404, on management's internal control assessment, appear?

options.A: Title IV, Enhanced Financial Disclosures
options.B: Title III, Corporate Responsibility
options.C: Title I, Public Company Accounting Oversight Board
options.D: Title IX, White-Collar Crime Penalty Enhancements

questions.key_concept: Section 404 sits in Title IV, Enhanced Financial Disclosures; Section 302 sits in Title III, Corporate Responsibility.
questions.pre_read: Recall how the Act's titles group its sections before matching one section to its title.
questions.correct_explanation: The Act's table of contents places Section 404, Management assessment of internal controls, in Title IV, Enhanced Financial Disclosures, with Sections 401 to 409. Title III, Corporate Responsibility, holds Section 301's audit committee rules and Section 302's officer certifications, which is why learners often file Section 404 there. Title I sets up the PCAOB, and Title IX holds Section 906's criminal certification.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Title III holds Section 302's certifications, which also touch internal control, but Section 404 sits in Title IV.
wrong_explanations.C: Title I establishes the PCAOB and its oversight of audit firms. It sets no issuer reporting duties such as Section 404.
wrong_explanations.D: Title IX raises white-collar penalties and adds Section 906's criminal certification. Section 404 is not a penalty provision.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Title I sets up the PCAOB, and D, because Title IX raises criminal penalties.
Final two: A beats B because Section 404 sits with the disclosure rules of Title IV; Title III holds Section 302's certifications.
Exam cue: in this Act the section number gives the title: 300s Corporate Responsibility, 400s Enhanced Financial Disclosures, 900s White-Collar Crime Penalty Enhancements.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Foreign private issuers. Test date
questions.question: Under Rule 3b-4, the general counsel of a foreign company that already reports to the SEC tests its foreign private issuer status each year as of:

options.A: the last day of its most recently completed fiscal year
options.B: the date it files its annual report on Form 20-F
options.C: the last business day of its most recent second fiscal quarter
options.D: the record date of its most recent annual meeting of shareholders

questions.key_concept: A reporting foreign company tests foreign private issuer status as of the last business day of its second fiscal quarter.
questions.pre_read: Recall which date the SEC uses to measure status during the year, as opposed to when the result applies.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 3b-4(c) applies the ownership and contact tests as of the last business day of the issuer's most recently completed second fiscal quarter, the same date used to measure public float. A new registrant instead tests within 30 days before its first registration statement (Rule 3b-4(d)). Option A is the natural guess, since filer status is fixed at year-end, but this test date falls mid-year.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: filer status is fixed at fiscal year-end, but the foreign private issuer test itself is measured at the end of the second fiscal quarter.
wrong_explanations.B: The test date is fixed in Rule 3b-4, not tied to a filing. The annual report comes months after the test date.
wrong_explanations.D: Rule 3b-4 counts holders of record as of a fixed quarter-end, not as of a shareholder meeting's record date.

tips: Eliminate: B and D, because Rule 3b-4 fixes one test date and ties it to neither a filing nor a shareholder meeting.
Final two: C beats A because the test runs at the end of the second fiscal quarter; only filer status is decided at year-end.
Exam cue: the mid-year date that measures public float also measures foreign private issuer status.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Foreign private issuers. Losing the status
questions.question: Kalmar Freight, a calendar-year foreign private issuer, fails the Rule 3b-4 test on its 30 June 2026 test date. From when must its reporting team use the forms for domestic issuers?

options.A: From 1 January 2027, the first day of its next fiscal year
options.B: From 1 July 2026, the day after its failed test date
options.C: From whenever the SEC staff notifies it of the change
options.D: Only after it fails the test again on 30 June 2027

questions.key_concept: A foreign private issuer that fails the test switches to domestic forms from the first day of its next fiscal year.
questions.pre_read: Separate the date the test is made from the date its result takes effect.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 3b-4(e) says a failed test governs the issuer's eligibility for the foreign private issuer forms and rules from the first day of the fiscal year after the test date. Kalmar keeps those forms for the rest of 2026 and moves to domestic forms, such as Forms 10-Q and 8-K, from 1 January 2027. Option B skips the transition the rule builds in.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the test is failed on 30 June, but Rule 3b-4(e) delays the change to the first day of the next fiscal year.
wrong_explanations.C: The issuer applies Rule 3b-4 itself, and the rule sets the switch date; no SEC notice is needed.
wrong_explanations.D: One failed test is enough. Rule 3b-4(e) applies the result from the next fiscal year without a second test.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the issuer applies Rule 3b-4 itself, and D, because one failed test is enough.
Final two: A beats B because Rule 3b-4(e) applies a failed test from the first day of the next fiscal year, not the day after the test.
Exam cue: a status measured mid-year changes the forms from the start of the next fiscal year.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Foreign private issuers. Canadian annual report form
questions.question: Maple Ridge Mines, an Ontario foreign private issuer reporting in Canada for six years, first registered with the SEC in 2025, with a $50 million public float. Which statement on Form 40-F is MOST accurate?

options.A: Yes; 12 months of Canadian reporting history is the deciding test
options.B: No; Form 40-F requires a public float of $75 million or more
options.C: No; Form 40-F is reserved for corporations owned by a Canadian government
options.D: Yes; any company incorporated in Canada may choose Form 40-F

questions.key_concept: Form 40-F needs Canadian incorporation, foreign private issuer status, 12 months of Canadian reporting and a $75 million public float.
questions.pre_read: List each eligibility condition for the Canadian form and test the company against every one.
questions.correct_explanation: Form 40-F General Instruction A.(2) lets a Canadian foreign private issuer or crown corporation use the form only if it has reported in Canada for at least 12 calendar months and has a public float of $75 million or more, unless it filed a Form F-9 by 30 Dec 2012. Maple Ridge meets the reporting test but not the float test, so it files Form 20-F. Option A stops at the first condition.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: 12 months of Canadian reporting is one condition, but Form 40-F also requires a public float of $75 million or more.
wrong_explanations.C: Crown corporations are one eligible group, but Canadian foreign private issuers can also qualify when they meet the reporting and float conditions.
wrong_explanations.D: Incorporation in Canada is only the first condition. The form also requires Canadian reporting history and a $75 million public float.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Canadian foreign private issuers can use the form too, and D, because incorporation in Canada is only the first condition.
Final two: B beats A because Form 40-F needs both 12 months of Canadian reporting and a public float of at least $75 million.
Exam cue: Form 40-F is a Canadian shortcut with a size floor; below it, a Canadian foreign private issuer files Form 20-F.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Foreign private issuers. Disclosure controls timing
questions.question: The CFO of Brisa SA, a foreign private issuer filing annual reports on Form 20-F, asks how often management must evaluate disclosure controls. What does Rule 13a-15(b) require?

options.A: An evaluation as of the end of each fiscal quarter
options.B: An evaluation each time the company furnishes a Form 6-K
options.C: No evaluation, since foreign private issuers are outside the rule
options.D: An evaluation as of the end of each fiscal year

questions.key_concept: A foreign private issuer's management evaluates disclosure controls as of each fiscal year-end, not each quarter.
questions.pre_read: Compare the domestic timing rule with any exception the rule gives foreign private issuers.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 13a-15(b) requires management, with the CEO and CFO taking part, to evaluate disclosure controls as of the end of each fiscal quarter, except that a foreign private issuer does so as of the end of each fiscal year. Form 20-F Item 15(a) then reports the officers' conclusions. Option A states the domestic rule, which the exception replaces for Brisa.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: quarterly evaluation is the rule for domestic issuers. Rule 13a-15(b)(1) sets a year-end evaluation for foreign private issuers.
wrong_explanations.B: Form 6-K carries furnished home-country news, not periodic reports. The rule ties the evaluation to the fiscal year, not to each 6-K.
wrong_explanations.C: Rule 13a-15 applies to every issuer with Section 12 registered securities; foreign private issuers get a timing accommodation, not an exemption.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Form 6-K does not set the evaluation timing, and C, because foreign private issuers get a timing accommodation, not an exemption.
Final two: D beats A because Rule 13a-15(b)(1) moves a foreign private issuer's evaluation to fiscal year-end; quarterly is the domestic rule.
Exam cue: foreign private issuer accommodations usually change timing to match the annual Form 20-F; they rarely remove a duty.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Registration and EDGAR. Size-based registration
questions.question: At fiscal year-end, Tidewell Robotics, a private company with $25 million in assets, has 1,300 holders of record of its common stock, including 600 non-accredited investors. What does Section 12(g) require?

options.A: Nothing, since only exchange-listed classes must ever register
options.B: Nothing yet, since the trigger is 2,000 holders of record
options.C: Registration within 120 days, as over 500 holders are non-accredited
options.D: A Securities Act registration statement before any further share sale

questions.key_concept: Section 12(g) requires registration when assets top $10 million and a class has 2,000 holders of record or 500 non-accredited holders.
questions.pre_read: Check the asset figure and both holder counts against the statute's thresholds.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 12(g)(1)(A) requires an issuer to register a class of equity within 120 days after the first fiscal year-end on which it has total assets over $10 million and the class is held of record by 2,000 persons or by 500 persons who are not accredited investors. Tidewell's 600 non-accredited holders trigger registration, which brings periodic reports and SOX duties. Option B misses the 500-person test.

wrong_explanations.A: Section 12(b) covers exchange listings, but Section 12(g) separately reaches unlisted companies that pass its asset and holder tests.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: 2,000 holders of record is one trigger, but 500 holders who are not accredited investors is an alternative trigger, and Tidewell has 600.
wrong_explanations.D: Securities Act registration covers an offering of securities. Section 12(g) registers the class itself because of its size and holder base.

tips: Eliminate: A, because Section 12(g) reaches unlisted companies, and D, because an offering registration is a different filing from Section 12(g) registration.
Final two: C beats B because Section 12(g) is met by 2,000 holders or by 500 non-accredited holders, once assets top $10 million.
Exam cue: Section 12(g) has two holder tests, 2,000 of record or 500 non-accredited, plus over $10 million in assets.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Registration and EDGAR. Suspended reporting
questions.question: Harlow Tools, a Section 15(d) filer never registered under Section 12, had 240 holders of record when this fiscal year began, years after its offering. What follows for its CFO's certifications on this year's reports?

options.A: None are due; its Section 15(d) duty is suspended for the year
options.B: None are due once the SEC grants an order ending its duty
options.C: They continue, as a Section 15(d) duty lasts while shares are held
options.D: They continue until its holders of record fall below 2,000

questions.key_concept: A Section 15(d) filer's reporting duty is suspended for a year that begins with fewer than 300 holders of record, and certifications fall away.
questions.pre_read: Find which provision makes the company report, then check when that duty can stop.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 15(d) automatically suspends the duty to file periodic reports for any fiscal year, other than the year the registration became effective, that begins with fewer than 300 holders of record of the class. With no periodic reports due for this year, there are no Section 302 certifications to sign. Rule 15d-6 asks only for a Form 15 notice within 30 days; Option B wrongly requires an SEC order.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Rule 15d-6 asks for a Form 15 notice within 30 days, but the statute suspends the duty automatically; no SEC order is needed.
wrong_explanations.C: A Section 15(d) duty is not permanent. The statute suspends it for any later fiscal year that begins with fewer than 300 holders of record.
wrong_explanations.D: 2,000 holders is a Section 12(g) registration trigger. The Section 15(d) suspension test is fewer than 300 holders at the start of the year.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the statute suspends a Section 15(d) duty below 300 holders, and D, because 2,000 holders is the Section 12(g) trigger.
Final two: A beats B because the suspension is automatic by statute; Rule 15d-6 asks only for a Form 15 notice.
Exam cue: SOX certifications ride on periodic reports; when the reporting duty is suspended, the certifications fall away with it.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Registration and EDGAR. Quarterly report deadline
questions.question: Under Rule 13a-13 and the Form 10-Q instructions, the controller of a non-accelerated filer must file each quarterly report within:

options.A: 40 days after the end of the fiscal quarter
options.B: 45 days after the end of the fiscal quarter
options.C: 60 days after the end of the fiscal quarter
options.D: four business days after the end of the fiscal quarter

questions.key_concept: A non-accelerated filer files each Form 10-Q within 45 days after the end of the fiscal quarter.
questions.pre_read: Place the company in its filer category first, then read the quarterly deadline for that category.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 13a-13 requires a Form 10-Q for each of the first three fiscal quarters, within the period in General Instruction A.1 of the form: 40 days after quarter-end for large accelerated and accelerated filers, and 45 days for all other registrants. A non-accelerated filer therefore has 45 days, and files no Form 10-Q for the fourth quarter. Option A is the accelerated filers' deadline.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: 40 days applies to large accelerated and accelerated filers. A non-accelerated filer falls under 'all other registrants', with 45 days.
wrong_explanations.C: 60 days is the large accelerated filer's deadline for the annual report on Form 10-K, not for a quarterly report.
wrong_explanations.D: Four business days is the usual deadline for a current report on Form 8-K about a listed event, not for a quarterly report.

tips: Eliminate: C, because 60 days is the large accelerated filer's Form 10-K deadline, and D, because four business days is the Form 8-K timeline.
Final two: B beats A because 40 days applies only to large accelerated and accelerated filers; every other registrant gets 45.
Exam cue: Form 10-Q deadlines have two tiers, 40 days for accelerated filers of either size and 45 for the rest, with no fourth-quarter 10-Q.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Registration and EDGAR. Getting EDGAR access
questions.question: Under Regulation S-T Rule 10, the reporting team of a company that has never filed on EDGAR must, before its first electronic filing:

options.A: mail a paper copy to the SEC for approval first
options.B: have its independent auditor register the company with the PCAOB
options.C: set up Login.gov credentials for staff, which alone give the company access
options.D: file Form ID, with a notarized document confirming the application

questions.key_concept: Before its first EDGAR filing, a company must file Form ID, the application for EDGAR access, with a notarized document.
questions.pre_read: Separate the company's application for EDGAR access from the sign-in credentials of the people who file for it.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 10(b) of Regulation S-T requires each electronic filer, before filing on EDGAR, to file Form ID, the application for EDGAR access, with a notarized document confirming it. Under EDGAR Next, the people who act for the company also sign in with Login.gov credentials, but those personal credentials do not give the company access on their own. Option C merges the two steps.

wrong_explanations.A: Regulation S-T requires electronic filing on EDGAR, and the SEC does not approve each filing before it is made. Paper is not the access step.
wrong_explanations.B: PCAOB registration is an audit firm's own duty under Section 102. It has nothing to do with a company's EDGAR access.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: individuals do need Login.gov credentials to sign in, but the company gets EDGAR access only after SEC staff grant its Form ID application.

tips: Eliminate: A, because Regulation S-T requires electronic filing, and B, because PCAOB registration concerns audit firms, not a company's EDGAR access.
Final two: D beats C because Rule 10(b) makes Form ID the company's application for access; Login.gov credentials only identify the people who act for it.
Exam cue: EDGAR is the system, Regulation S-T is the rule, and Form ID is the application to use the system.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 American Depositary Receipts. Staying exempt at Level 1
questions.question: Under Rule 12g3-2(b), the CFO of a foreign private issuer with an over-the-counter Level 1 ADR program keeps the company exempt from Section 12(g) registration by:

options.A: furnishing each home-country report to the SEC on Form 6-K
options.B: filing an annual report on Form 20-F within four months
options.C: publishing its home-country disclosures online in English
options.D: having its depositary bank register the ADRs on Form F-6

questions.key_concept: A Level 1 issuer keeps its Rule 12g3-2(b) exemption by publishing its home-country disclosures in English online.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether the company reports to the SEC at all, then match each option to that status.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 12g3-2(b) exempts a foreign private issuer from Section 12(g) registration if it does not report under Section 13(a) or 15(d), keeps a foreign listing that is its primary trading market, and publishes its home-country disclosures in English online. Rule 12g3-2(b)(2) makes that publication ongoing to keep the exemption. Option A describes reporting issuers, which furnish home-country news on Form 6-K.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Form 6-K is how reporting foreign private issuers furnish home-country news. Rule 12g3-2(b) serves issuers that do not report and asks for online publication.
wrong_explanations.B: Filing Form 20-F annual reports would make the company a reporting issuer, the status the exemption lets it avoid.
wrong_explanations.D: Form F-6 registers the ADRs under the Securities Act. It is available because of the exemption; it does not create the exemption.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Form 20-F annual reports make a company a reporting issuer, and D, because Form F-6 registers only the ADRs.
Final two: C beats A because Rule 12g3-2(b) is for non-reporting issuers and requires English publication online; Form 6-K belongs to reporting issuers.
Exam cue: Level 1 rests on Rule 12g3-2(b): a home listing as the primary market, English disclosure online and no SEC periodic reports.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Registration and EDGAR. EDGAR outage on a due date
questions.question: On its Form 10-Q due date, a company's reporting team hits unexpected technical problems that block its EDGAR submission. Under Regulation S-T Rule 201, what may the team do?

options.A: Email the report to SEC staff, which then counts as filed
options.B: File Form 12b-25 to give notice that the report will be late
options.C: Nothing; electronic filing has no exception, so the report is late
options.D: File it on paper under Form TH within one business day

questions.key_concept: Rule 201 lets a filer blocked by unanticipated technical difficulties file on paper under Form TH within one business day.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the rules give a fallback for technical failure, and which notice belongs to which problem.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 201 of Regulation S-T gives a temporary hardship exemption: a filer whose electronic filing is blocked by unanticipated technical difficulties may file in paper, under cover of Form TH, no later than one business day after the due date, and the report counts as filed on time. An electronic copy follows within six business days. The rule bars using Form 12b-25 for electronic difficulties, so Option B fails.

wrong_explanations.A: Email is not a filing method. Apart from the Rule 201 paper route, reports must go through EDGAR under Regulation S-T.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Form 12b-25 notifies late filings in general, but Rule 201 says filers blocked by electronic difficulties must use the hardship route instead.
wrong_explanations.C: Rule 201 is the exception: a paper filing under Form TH within one business day counts as filed by the due date.

tips: Eliminate: A, because email is not a filing method, and C, because Rule 201 gives a temporary hardship exemption.
Final two: D beats B because Rule 201 covers technical difficulties and bars using Form 12b-25 for them.
Exam cue: Regulation S-T requires EDGAR; Rule 201 is its short paper fallback for technical failures, with an electronic copy to follow.
