questions.subtopic: 1A5 American Depositary Receipts. Level 1 at a reporting company
questions.question: Sorrento SpA files Form 20-F annual reports because of a registered 2023 U.S. bond offering, and now adds an over-the-counter Level 1 ADR program. Which statement about its officers' certifications is MOST accurate?

options.A: They stop; a Level 1 program needs only Form F-6
options.B: They continue; its own Section 15(d) reporting still requires them
options.C: They stop; ADR holders cannot rely on officer certifications
options.D: They continue only if the ADR program later becomes Level 2

questions.key_concept: Certifications follow the company's own periodic reporting, not the ADR level; a reporting company keeps certifying after adding a Level 1 program.
questions.pre_read: Find what makes the company file reports, then ask whether the ADR program changes that.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 302 certifications follow the company's own periodic reports, not its ADR level. Sorrento files Form 20-F under Section 15(d) because of its registered bond offering, so its CEO and CFO keep certifying each annual report. Form F-6 is open to an issuer that already reports (17 CFR 239.36(c)). Option A applies the Level 1 picture of a company that relies on Rule 12g3-2(b) and files no reports.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a Level 1 program itself needs only Form F-6, but Sorrento already reports under Section 15(d), and that reporting carries the certifications.
wrong_explanations.C: Certifications attach to the periodic report, whoever holds the securities. Sorrento's Form 20-F still needs them.
wrong_explanations.D: Level 2 would add an exchange listing, but Sorrento's duty already exists through its Section 15(d) reporting.

tips: Eliminate: C, because certifications attach to the report, not to the holders, and D, because Sorrento's duty already exists without a listing.
Final two: B beats A because the Form F-6-only picture fits a non-reporting Level 1 company; Sorrento reports under Section 15(d).
Exam cue: follow the company's own reporting, not the ADR level; a reporting company keeps certifying whatever its ADR program.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. Who a loan ban covers
questions.question: A listed manufacturer that does no consumer lending reviews four proposed personal loans, each on market terms. Under Section 402, which loan may the company make?

options.A: A loan to a plant manager who is not an executive officer
options.B: A loan to an outside director who sits on the audit committee
options.C: A 90-day bridge loan to the CFO, repaid before year-end
options.D: A loan to the general counsel, approved by the full board

questions.key_concept: Section 402 bars personal loans to directors and executive officers only; other employees fall outside it.
questions.pre_read: Check each borrower's role first, then whether any exception in the section fits.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 402 added Exchange Act Section 13(k), which makes it unlawful for an issuer, directly or through a subsidiary, to extend or arrange a personal loan to any director or executive officer. A plant manager who is not an executive officer is outside the ban. Option B fails because the section names every director, not just employees or executives; an outside director is still a director.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an outside director is not an employee, but Section 402 bans personal loans to any director as well as executive officers.
wrong_explanations.C: Section 402 has no short-term or bridge loan exception. The CFO is an executive officer, so the loan is barred.
wrong_explanations.D: Board approval does not cure the ban. The general counsel is an executive officer, so the loan is barred.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Section 402 has no bridge-loan exception, and D, because board approval does not lift the ban.
Final two: A beats B because Section 402 reaches every director and executive officer; an outside director is still a director.
Exam cue: find the actor first; the loan ban covers directors and executive officers, not every employee.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. Lawyers the attorney rules reach
questions.question: A listed company's general counsel is mapping which of its lawyers the SEC's attorney conduct rules under Section 307 cover. Which lawyer is appearing and practicing before the Commission?

options.A: A staff lawyer who handles only the company's workplace injury claims
options.B: None of its staff lawyers, since the rules reach only outside counsel
options.C: A staff lawyer advising which contracts to file with the 10-K
options.D: A foreign lawyer advising only on home-country law, outside U.S. matters

questions.key_concept: The SEC's Section 307 rules cover any lawyer, in-house or outside, who advises an issuer on what goes in its SEC filings.
questions.pre_read: Look at what each lawyer actually does for the issuer, not whether they are employed or retained.
questions.correct_explanation: Under 17 CFR 205.2, appearing and practicing before the Commission includes advising an issuer whether information must be filed with the SEC, and representing an issuer covers lawyers whether employed or retained by it. A staff lawyer advising on what to file with the 10-K is covered. Option B is the common belief that only outside counsel count; the definition expressly includes in-house lawyers.

wrong_explanations.A: Workplace injury work has no link to SEC filings, investigations or securities law advice, so it is not appearing and practicing before the Commission.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: outside counsel are often covered, but Rule 205.2 covers lawyers representing an issuer whether employed or retained, so in-house lawyers count.
wrong_explanations.D: A non-appearing foreign attorney, who gives no advice on U.S. law and acts only incidentally to foreign practice, is excluded from the rules.

tips: Eliminate: A, because workplace injury work involves no SEC matter, and D, because non-appearing foreign attorneys are excluded.
Final two: C beats B because Rule 205.2 covers lawyers whether employed or retained by the issuer; in-house advice on a filing counts.
Exam cue: under Section 307, ask what the lawyer does (SEC filings, inquiries, securities advice), not who pays them.
